utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before continuing where we stopped last Friday, I have a few questions in respect of the 92 bis statements. The -- well, let me say, the new statements have been filed approximately two weeks ago. I did not see any response to that from the Defence. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the response will come in the course of this week, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But is it not seven days that the Rules give you for a response? After notification, and I take that filing the documents is --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This motion was dated 31st of May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was the 92 bis statements were filed -- I haven't got exactly in my mind at this moment, but I remember it was Thursday or Friday two weeks ago

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It was the six of June. If I may assist. The Prosecution filed, this morning, some further submissions which seek to apply the principals of the Appeals Chamber judgment of the 7th of June. So assuming that that is acceptable to the Trial Chamber, I think I indicated last week that we would do that. The Prosecution would have no objection to the Defence having an opportunity to respond to those submissions filed this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Since the Chamber has to hear the parties, apart from any responses, we would like to find a moment during this week. So could you please take care that, let's say on from Wednesday, that you are prepared to make any oral arguments you would additionally like to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I respectfully suggest Thursday as an appropriate day. Tomorrow we have witness AD. I anticipate evidence in chief would be of the order of three hours. So we should finish him easily by Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Thursday is after Wednesday, so you are all prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is acceptable for the Defence, Mr. President. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Then -- but there is another issue. We still have to deal with the documents that are tendered during the testimony of the expert witness, Dr. -- Professor Zecevic. Madam Registrar, would you please guide through the documents. Us

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have Prosecutor's Exhibit 3721, which is sketch number 1 and Prosecutor's Exhibit 3722, which is sketch number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before we proceed from there may I respectfully ask that the full statement of the expert witness filed the 11th of April 2002 be also received in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it has been filed as the expert report on the basis of which he was examined and cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that was, Mr. Stamp, number -- you mentioned a number, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That would be 3723. P3723.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the Exhibit tendered by the Prosecution, 3494, a statement by Mr. Zecevic, the 26th and 27th of October, and reference numbers are given too fast by the counsel. The Defence is objecting to this part being submitted and tendered as evidence because in this part of the statement, Mr. Berko Zecevic is speaking about air bombing, air bombs, and we believe that this part of the statement of Mr. Zecevic is not relevant to the case of the General Galic. So for this reason, we believe that this part of the statement cannot be exhibit of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any response to that, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We could deal with that matter in any way which is convenient to the Court. That part of the statement was left in out of an abundance of caution because the Rule refers to the full statement. So we did not think that, without any leave from the Court, we ought to redact anything from it. If the Court so orders, we will be prepared to redact that aspect, however I think that the matter is before the Court and the Court is entitled to review it and to use whatever parts of it it deems relative and probative. However, I am in the hands of the Court. It could be a solution found one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would the parties agree that there is no direct relevance in that part of the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the parties would agree if we would either ask you to provide us a copy with stricken out that part of it, or that we would decide that we would admit the -- admit the statement in evidence, but not in respect of the -- that part of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Any way it pleases the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will give a decision on that after the break. I mean, it seems to be a rather technical matter by now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would prefer, also in order to avoid whatever risk of contamination of our minds, that the exhibit would be redacted to the extent as just discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Being there is nothing else at this very moment, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. President. I call Dr. Stuart Turner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could you -- yes, I see you are already active.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: While he is coming, Mr. President, I propose to show him a copy of his report, simply in order for him to identify it and the report contains his education and qualifications. Unless you think it necessary, I will rely upon that appendix, number I, as the qualifying of him as an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, always of course will be a possibility of cross-examining the witness. But I don't think it is necessary to have him repeat everything in appendix I.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, would you prefer that he was shown a copy from the bar table or the actual copy which has been filed, which I assume Madam Registrar has?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that these copies are made from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Turner, I presume. Yes. I take it that you understand me in a language -- that you can hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like you to ask you to put in your earphones because someone might say something in a language that you do not understand and you will certainly need these earphones, unless you speak fluent Bosnian, Serbian, Croatian and French.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps you should put on your earphones. Before giving testimony in this court, I take it that you understand the English language at this moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving testimony in this court the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text of this declaration will be handed out to you -- is already handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Turner. Please be seated. Dr. Turner, you will first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. I see that you are putting something which I cannot see from here on your table. Unless it is white paper where you would like to make some notes. If there is anything else, you certainly will be asked to or something will be put in front of you if necessary. And if there is anything that you would like to consult, please ask permission to do so. Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Turner are you a psychiatrist by profession, with rooms in Harley Street in London in the United Kingdom?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the witness be shown a copy of his report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, would you please go to appendix I of the report which commences on page 23. Commencing on page 23, do you set out your various educational qualifications including postgraduate training and your main appointments previous appointments, and other activities?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 23, under the subheading "Court Work," you referred to having received training as a single joint expert. Could you tell us briefly what a "single joint expert" is in the context of civil litigation in the United Kingdom?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: A single joint expert is an expert appointed by the court in the setting of personal injury litigation. A single expert is there to advise the court, not to take one side or another, indeed, no expert should take one side or another. But a single expert is appointed by the court to prepare a psychiatric assessment, which both parties have agreed to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when did you first qualify as a psychiatrist?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I became a consultant psychiatrist in 1987.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you since then developed expertise in the area of trauma?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I have. In fact, I was working in trauma somewhat before then, as a psychiatrist, but have since then developed a national centre for the treatment of people with traumatic stress reactions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise the document as a whole to be a report prepared by you and dated the 6th of May 2002?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I do. And it was this report by the way, Mr. President, that I had taken from my bag, which I have now put back into my bag. I am sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I expected as a matter of fact, but you are confronted by the copy provided to you by the Court -- by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does your signature appear on page 22?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: It appears on page 22.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that completes examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. It happens that we received the B/C/S version rather belatedly of this interesting document. We are going to ask for leave to cross-examine in tandem, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, do you have -- because we have not ruled yet on the time you would take, could you be, perhaps after having prepared cross-examination, be more precise, we gave you a guideline at that time that it would -- that the efforts would be 50 per cent of what you estimate was?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this witness was supposed to last for two and a half hours, the examination of the witness would last for two and a half hours, if I remember correctly, and it was for this reason that we prepared. But I think that we will probably go below this time. I would just confer. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About two hours, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, even if it is in tandem.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't know yet because we were very surprised by the very short time taken for examination-in-chief so we don't know who is going to start first. It will be Ms. Pilipovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Turner, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turner, in your report that you submitted to the Court on the 6th of May 2002, under item 1, you said that you gave your expert opinion on the problem that you were given and that you worked out that this was based on your qualifications and your work experience. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: My expert opinion is based on qualifications, my experience, and my instruction.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Turner. Now, Mr. Turner, not going into your qualifications, I would like us to clarify your work with the courts. On page 26 of your report, that is, in the translation into B/C/S, that is 0305461 of the translation, but you said, and I believe that you will agree with me, that approximately 5 per cent of your work so far is in connection to legal -- to litigation cases and criminal cases.

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I think there is a problem with translation. Litigation is not -- is not quite accurate. In my report, I set out that about 5 per cent of my current work is in criminal or family court cases. That is distinct from litigation, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand the difference you make because you are talking about approximately equal number assigned cases or civil litigation. And you are talking about litigation, so not all your court work is litigation, that is what you want to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, I do take it that you were referring to, at least a part of the 5 per cent where court work is not always mentioned litigation. So, if it is a matter of translation, then could you please repeat your question and let's hope that no confusion comes up.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turner, 5 per cent of your work so far has been in connection for either criminal or for family courts. Could you be precise, please.

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I would agree that 5 -- about 5 per cent of my work is in connection with criminal and family courts. I am not sure I can be more precise than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Turner, could you tell us in relation to this 5 per cent of your work that you gave specification for, could you tell us, what per Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. cent is linked to criminal cases?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I suppose, as an estimate, I would say probably about the same amount of criminal and family work. So probably about two and a half, two per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Turner, could you tell us what did you give your expert opinion on when we are talking about criminal cases? When I say that, what I mean is, if you can answer whether you gave your expert opinion on the state of mind of the perpetrator or the state of mind of the victim? And if you gave your opinion on the -- both, both perpetrators and the victim could you give us then how many of one cases and how many of the other, and also before which courts did you testify as an expert.

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: When I talk about criminal cases I am talking about my role as assessor of the perpetrator or the alleged perpetrator. And I am talking about giving evidence before a criminal court in which the perpetrator is being prosecuted. There may, in addition, over and above this, be matters of civil redress either through a compensation authority or through litigation. But that would be what I have dealt with under another category. When I am talking about criminal court work, I am talking about the assessment of a perpetrator or alleged perpetrator, in the context of Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turner, thank you. Now, could you, with this answer, can confirm that you did not give -- you did not testify, did not give evidence, in cases where you were an expert, you did not assess the state of mind of a victim that is, the psychological state of mind of a person who suffered consequences as a result of being a victim, of having been a victim?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: No. The vast majority of my work involves assess the state of mind of victims. But that would not be dealt with in the United Kingdom in the setting of a criminal court. That would be dealt with in other settings. That's why I separated it out. It would be dealt with, for example, in the setting of someone seeking, seeking compensation as a victim or someone seeking asylum because of being victimised in another place. That's the majority of my work.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turner, could you tell us in your field of work, how did you assess the state of mind of a victim? When I say that, what I mean is, was the objective of your examination -- were these the victims who suffered fear because of what has been done to them? Did they suffer pain and so on?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: In the vast majority of my work, what I have to do is to assess the mental state of people, as a psychiatrist. So I am interested in looking at their emotional state or other aspects of the person, to try to determine, as best I can as a psychiatrist, whether they may have an injury as a consequence of a particular experience. And if they have an injury, its nature, its cause, its treatment, its severity.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Turner. Since you confirm that, in your work, you also testified on the state of mind, you gave evidence on the state of mind of the victim, could you tell us your opinion, did you make it just based on the data and written documents, or did you also base your opinion on using psychiatric methods?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I am a psychiatrist, so when I'm asked to give evidence on the state of mind of a victim, then my normal practice would be to carry out a psychiatric assessment, to interview, to examine the mental state, and to look at a bundle of relevant documents, including, where possible, past medical records or other contemporaneous notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us which psychiatric methods do you use when you are giving evidence in courts? Giving your expert evidence in courts. Do you use interview? Do you use observation for a longer period of time? Do you use psychological tests?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: To some degree, it depends on the nature of the problem. But if I am examining a victim, then I would normally interview. I use a semi-structured assessment of mental state, based on a particular diagnostic system, the diagnostic and statistical manual. Sometimes self-report measures or personality questionnaires or other assessment tools are required. But it depends a lot on the nature of the problem that I am being asked to comment on.

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: Mr. Turner, would you agree with me that a serious psychiatric analysis of victims that are supposed to examine in order to find fear, it cannot be done without a direct interview with the victims or a victim?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: If I am being asked to assess an individual or court case, my normal practice would be to interview that individual. I think that if I am being asked to comment on the effect on a population, which I think is what I am being asked to do here, then different methods are appropriate. It would not be possible for me to interview a population.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand your answer, Mr. Turner. Could you, perhaps, tell us whether what would be needed would be a sample, and what would be the sample that you would need, in relation to a whole population, in order to come to your conclusions? For instance if we assume that a population is 300.000 people, how many people would you need for a sample, for you to interview in order to give your opinion, for the whole of this population?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: That is not an answer that I can simply provide. Scientifically, if we were looking at a whole population, which I want to qualify, but if we were looking at a whole population, then it would be reasonable to carry out a survey of a sample of that population. Scientifically, there is something called a "power analysis" which is a way of identifying what the sample size should be. The power analysis depends upon prior estimation from previous surveys of the likely scale of disturbance. If the likely scale of disturbance is high, then the sample size required for a scientific analysis is relatively small. If the estimated disturbance is low, then the sample is correspondingly larger. That is a power analysis. To calculate a power analysis would require a computer. It's a fairly standard approach, but not something I can answer here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turner, would you agree with me that the expert witness's opinion should be completely truthful, correct, and based on facts?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When I say "fully," I would like you to confirm to us whether you took into consideration all the relevant facts in order to do your report?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I took into consideration all the facts known to me. I must qualify at this point and say that some of the material provided to me, I qualify in my report because some of it is based on witness evidence or allegation. It is not for me to say whether those are facts. But I do qualify that in one of the early paragraphs of my report. But this report is prepared on any information that I thought was relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turner can you tell us what information did you assess to be relevant, as an expert, in order to write your report?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I carried out -- I looked at the material provided for me in my instruction, which I set out in the report. I looked at the witness material provided to me. But the main focus of my report was on the scientific literature, which is material that I have reasonable familiarity with. But in any case, I conducted computerized searches to try to identify additional material with which I, perhaps, hadn't been familiar beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turner, under point 9 of your report, page 4 of the translation, but it is also point 9 in the English version, you said that you had to work on the basis of the assumption that the Prosecution would broadly establish the facts contained in the indictment from which you drew your facts. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: It is roughly correct. What I say there is that I am quoting from an indictment, the indictment includes material which the Prosecution has to establish at trial. It is not for an expert witness to determine if that material is right or wrong. That's for the Court. And I am qualifying my report explicitly by saying that I am aware that this is something which the Court will have to determine, as I go through my opinion. But the bulk of my opinion is based on trying to find -- trying to look at the scientific literature and see how it relates to some of that witness evidence. What I say here is if the Tribunal does not broadly accept this material, then some of the conclusions I may draw on the basis of that material should also not be accepted. I tried to make that explicit in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Turner. Could you tell us which facts, which are the facts which the Prosecution must prove so that your opinion can be accepted?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: What I set out here is material from an indictment, for example, in paragraph 8, I quote from the first schedule to the indictment, describing 27 incidents involving shooting of civilians. And in the second schedule, five incidents of shelling of civilian groups. For example, the shelling of a football game, civilian group waiting for water and so on. Now, my job is not to say whether those incidents happened or didn't happen, but I need to offer the Court advice on the assumption that they may have happened and how might people have reacted to that sort of experience. That is what I try to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Turner do you consider that the findings of your report and your opinion are objective, based on the premises that still have not been proved?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I think my report is objective and I set out any qualifications that I think are appropriate in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Turner, under point 36, page 23, of your opinion report, you state -- quote a document which you refer to -- you speak about a document given by the author John -- an author by the name of John. Could you perhaps clarify on the basis of which opinion or which literature you provided information under item 36? Specifically, I am referring to the Kosevo hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I assume that the reference to "John" is probably a reference to Jones which appears in the third line of the English version of the report at paragraph 36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that correct, Ms. Pilipovic? So John should be Jones?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That is right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a reference to a published report in the British Medical Journal and at the very end of my report, I give a list of citations, including the reference of this report by Jones, 1995, published in the British Medical Journal with the page reference and volume number. As I say, I did look through the medical literature with a computerized search. This report was a report that came through as being of relevance to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turner, is this a -- the report that you refer to, is it a letter from Sarajevo on pages 1052 and 1054. Is that literature a part of your report which you, in fact, refer to and can you tell us whether it is question of a two-page letter, published in the mentioned medical journal?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: It is an article which has a title, "Letter from Sarajevo." That is not the same as saying it is a published letter, as would normally be understood in the academic press. But it is an article from Dr. Jones in Sarajevo. And as material in the published literature, it seemed of relevance to mention it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turner, in that article which you used as literature, did you come to information regarding assistance of psychiatric patients at the Kosevo hospital?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: She talks about the situation in the Kosevo hospital and talks about the help offered to psychiatric patients, and the change in pattern of presentation of those patients.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turner, did you have occasion to inform yourself about medical documentation which was used by Mrs. Jones when writing her report or letter?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: It is Dr. Jones, for the translation, not "Mrs. Jones." She is a psychiatrist. No, I don't know -- it would not be normal practice to try to seek information underpinning a report in a peer review journal like the British Medical Journal. Normally the practice would be to look at the report itself, which is what I have done.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, Dr. Turner, you were never in a situation to deal with official data regarding people who were patients of the Kosevo hospital?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I don't believe I have come across a reference providing that information, so, no, the answer is: What I have seen about the Kosevo hospital is what is described in the medical literature.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turner, in your report, under point 10, you said that while you were studying external sources, you came across many reports containing similar descriptions. When I am saying this and mentioning a great number of reports, are these reports of the medical services in Sarajevo that you used, given the information you provided under item 10?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I have -- I would regard the report by Dr. Jones who was working in Bosnia as being a report from the medical service in Sarajevo. I have also seen literature, for example, prepared more anecdotally by Dr. Aitcheson [phoen] who was a former chief medical officer in the United Kingdom, who visited Sarajevo during this period. I am aware of more anecdotal literature. And I have spoken to people who have worked there. But what I cited here is some material where there is some numerical description or quantification. I think that is of more relevance to the Court. But there is other material describing experiences in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Turner, you told us that Dr. Jones worked in Sarajevo. Could you tell us whether you are aware when she worked in Sarajevo, and for how long did she stay and work in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I can't answer that question, I am afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say you can't answer that question, does that mean that you don't know when she worked in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I can't give you the date of her working from when to when in Sarajevo, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turner, you have just told us that Dr. Aitcheson [phoen] also lived in Sarajevo, stayed in Sarajevo, and that you used his findings as well in connection with the victims. Could you tell us when he went to Sarajevo, for what period and what data, which data did you use from Dr. Aitcheson's [phoen] report or findings?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: It is Dr. Aitcheson [phoen]. Dr. Aitcheson [phoen] was in Bosnia -- again, I can't give you exact dates, I'm afraid, but roughly 1992 and 1993. And I think that what he provides is not data, but another description and it is that to which I am referring in paragraph 10. I am talking about literature with similar descriptions. He gives descriptions of escorting a food convoy and coming under gunfire. He gives descriptions of trying to organise medical relief through WHO. He gives descriptions of some of his experiences and impressions in Sarajevo. But his report is a more impressionistic descriptive paper, without the benefit of the numbers that come through in Dr. Jones report. But I could have cited Dr. Aitcheson [phoen]. I don't regard those reports as being in conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turner, under item 10, when you say in line 2, example, in one report of the medical services in Sarajevo during the siege undertaken in May 1993, it was stated that the daily bombardment and sniper fire directed at civilians had caused a steady stream of casualties. Mr. Turner, were you able to see that medical report which you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I have seen that report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So the report that you tell us that you had seen, could you tell us whether it, that report was an integral part of Dr. Jones' letter? If not, could you tell us that the medical report was enclosed by you, along Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with your expertise? In other words, could you give us some more information about the medical report you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: This is not the same as Dr. Jones' letter. And again, if I can draw the attention to the Court to the reference list at the end. This is a separate paper published in a different journal, Prehospital and Disaster Medicine by Pretto et al. This report, I have read and it is another report which included numbers dealing with the casualties in Sarajevo. The report was undertaken in May 1993 and it reported some of the data from Sarajevo. I presume that data came from official sources. Without going back and checking the report again, I can't give a precise answer to that. But the way the report was set out, it included details on each of the surgical units in Sarajevo with numbers of people presenting and the operation rates and so on. So, it was a very detailed assessment particularly of a particular month, which was November 1992, but it wasn't restricted to that month.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turner, if I understood you correctly, you didn't look at the medical report, but that you used an article which you invoked, an article by Mr. Begovic, Pretto and his associates in 1994?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: The report is a report in a journal, that is the nature of a medical report. It is published in a journal and it is open for all to look at and all to challenge. I have looked at that report. I have read it in detail. The first author of that report was Pretto. Co-authors included Begovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turner, when you used that report, does that mean that you used data from that report but you did not verify whether the reports were true or not, when you were writing your own report?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I think there is a misunderstanding here and it might be helpful to try to clarify. When a paper is submitted to a journal like the British Medical Journal or another journal for publication, the paper is looked at carefully to see if it is a paper that that journal feels is accurate and helpful, see if it meets certain scientific criteria and so on. So the journal carries a responsibility to make sure that it is not publishing material which is misleading or incorrect. Having published the journal -- the article in the journal, if the journal discovers that it has inadvertently published something which may be misleading or incorrect, the journal has a clear obligation to correct itself. Therefore, this is material which, in medical practice, it is normal to quote.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turner, by using this medical journal, did you have an opportunity to contact the people who compiled this report, medical report, so-called, in order to check the accuracy of the data that was included in their report, or the article that was published as a medical report?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: As I have already explained, that responsibility and that discussion takes place between the journal editor and the reviewers that the editor calls in to help and the authors of the paper. Once it is published in the scientific literature, then normal practice is that the article would then be quoted. Indeed, it is hard to see how someone like myself could now go back and try and check whether this material was accurate. I presume that this is -- this is the discussion that happened at the time of publication. It is not something which would be easy to do now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turner, when you prepared your report, so you used the literature that you quoted, that you referred to, that you gave a list of together with your report, specifically speaking, when we are talking about the data of the victims published in the medical journal that you used and that you quoted, do you have an opportunity when you were preparing your expert report, did you have an opportunity to also acquaint yourself with other reports, in relation to the number of victims the victims of the war in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: As I said, the method that I used was to look at the material that I knew. But to go back and to do a computerized search of a compilation database, to see if there was material I hadn't been familiar with, I have done that and I have cited material which seemed relevant. If there had been material, which I came across, which gave a different picture, then that material would also have been quoted.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When we are talking about data, the numbers of victims for the relevant period in Sarajevo, that is, 1992 to 1994 could you tell us what other sources of data did you use when we are talking about the numbers of victims?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: The material that I have -- was interested in looking at the numbers of victims, I quoted. It wasn't -- this was not a primary purpose of my report though. And again it seems that this is a substance of the court to determine whether these incidents did take place and whether the shooting and the injuries did happen. It is published in the medical literature. The Court may wish to listen to that or it may not wish to listen to that. I was more interested, in preparing this report, in some of the ways that people reacted to some of those experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you wanted to check the way that the people reacted to some of these experiences, are you saying, when you say, "people," do you mean persons like Dr. Jones, who wrote a report about the situation in the hospitals in Sarajevo, and other persons who followed the situation of people during that period? So, not you personally.

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I was instructed that this case is to do with the reaction and the experience of civilians in Sarajevo during this particular period, and that the particular issue is whether those civilians may or may not have been terrorised during this particular period. That was the issue that I chose, on the basis of instruction, to try to focus on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So, what you are saying is that your instructions, your task, was to study whether the civilians in Sarajevo were terrorised. In your report in item 4 of your report, you gave a definition of a terrorist. Could you briefly explain the importance of the terms, "terror", "terrorism", "terrorise" and "terrorist"?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I think the importance of these terms is to do with legal application and I don't think I am best qualified to comment on that side. But what I quoted here was from a standard dictionary in the United Kingdom. It is a reputable source. Some simple definitions of these words which I thought were helpful in going through this issue. So I defined -- the dictionary defines terror as a state of extreme fear. It defines a terrorist as one who favours or uses terror inspiring methods of governing or of coercing either government or community and to terrorise is to fill with terror or to coerce by terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turner, do you believe that the operation of the Bosnian Serb forces under General Galic, in the time relevant for the indictment in its primary aim, was it a terrorist one? Was it with an objective of terrorising the population?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: Again, I think that is a matter for the Court. What I tried to do is to say, if these facts were accepted by the Court, what would the implications be. I don't think it is for me to determine that answer, but that is clearly a crucial question for the Court to determine.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has finished this part of the cross-examination. My colleague will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. So that we are in check with the hours, could you tell us when is the next break, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next break will be at a quarter to 4.00. So that is approximately 20 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am going to go back to the methodology that you used. We saw in your report that you quoted, in places, some of the transcripts and the first question will be the following: Did you have access to all of the transcripts in relation to this case?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, if I can draw your attention to paragraph 2 of my report, I set out the source material and make it quite plain that I have had access to extracts, both of the trial brief and that I had originally been provided with extracts from witness statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: That is exactly the reason -- that is the reason why I am asking you this question, sir. You said you had access to pieces, assorted pieces in some way. But were you able to have access to the res?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I have not had access to the rest. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: -- Attention to that in paragraph 2, so that the report is not misleading to the Court in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Doctor, this is not a criticism on my part. We are just trying to establish what is what. Now, Doctor, were there cases, for instance, whereby - and I hope you will be able to answer by a yes or no - the Prosecution may have given you excerpts that would have established for instance, that the Muslim forces were firing on their own citizens in order to create losses; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: The material that I -- I am not going to answer it yes or no, if I can. The material that I was given initially was to do with extracts from witness statements. My understanding is that those extracts were sourced on the basis of reference to a psychological reaction. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, I am going to have to interrupt you. I am so sorry. But the question was very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, Dr. Turner, whether you do it in a yes or no, but that you could answer the question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was trying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry. What I was going to say is that I can't recall whether that material included evidence of one sort or another in that way. I have to say that I can't recall being provided with evidence to do with actions by the Muslim authorities of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Doctor. Now, did you ever have in your hands testimonies, according to which you would have -- the testimonies which would have said that Muslim forces were firing on their own funeral precession?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing such testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Doctor, were you given any testimonies or statements of, for instance, of high representatives of the UN forces in Bosnia, and the testimonies would say that the Muslim forces were either exploiting human misery or were manipulating the media and that they were using this as a weapon of war?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing such testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Doctor, when you say that you do not recall, does this mean clearly that you were never given these elements?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I have already said that I had been given little extracts from a number of witness statements. So whether they include or didn't include, I can't give a dogmatic answer to, but I don't recall seeing it. Therefore, my assumption was I wasn't provided with --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Doctor, Doctor, you have a very good memory, no doubt. Am I to interpret your answer as being the fact that you were never given such elements? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I have answered that. I can't recall being given such elements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the last part of the previous answer was that it was the assumption of the witness, since he has no recollection of having seen such information, that he has not been provided with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is true. Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Doctor, did you yourself ever take an initiative to be able to have access to other sources of information rather than only the ones that you were provided by?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: The bulk of my report is to do with emotional reactions to a particular situation. I have taken initiative to look at the published literature on that subject. The facts of the matter in terms of what happened are a backdrop, that is for the Court to determine, not for an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Doctor, I am going to have to interrupt you again. I am sorry. Doctor, is it true that you accepted selected excerpts that were given to you by the Prosecution; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am not sure why I have to keep on being interrupted. I am trying to answer these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Stuart, we have a problem in this court and that is time. So, therefore, Mr. Piletta-Zanin knows exactly if he uses too much time, that he might be stopped from further asking questions. Therefore, if your answers are not, at least at first, I shouldn't say aside, but at first hearing, not go in the direction of the question, Mr. Piletta-Zanin tries to bring you back to the question. If, however, there is any specific aspect you say, "my answer is not well understandable unless I give a certain explanation," please ask permission to do so. I am certain that you will get an opportunity. The main question of Mr. Piletta-Zanin is: Is your report based on material that was exclusively selected by the Prosecution, as a matter of facts, or whether any -- did you ask for anything extra, did you feel unhappy with being provided with the selection you had no control over, that is, I think, the main issue, Mr. Piletta-Zanin is asking you. But, before answering that question could I ask you, approximately how many pages, let's say, of excerpts you received? Was that 50 or 100 or 500 or 1.000? Just approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The excerpts were about four lines each, five lines each and probably 20 or 30 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So taken out of a -- of a witness testimony --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, witness statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you say statements. You say you start would the statements and then you went on with the testimony of the witness in court. And I have seen several quotes of what witnesses have said in court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Material provided here was material provided rather later. And the great majority of the material I have been provided with is included here. So there wasn't a great deal more than you can see here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So, but I just wanted you to answer my question, Doctor, please. Did you yourself ask for a possibility to have access to a deeper source, to a more extensive source, of documents?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I did discuss that, yes. I am told that the deeper source is enormous and there were some practical issues about being able to make meaningful use of that. I am also aware that the deeper sources are to do with the facts, rather than with the psychiatric implications. So I didn't feel particularly troubled by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Doctor what do you know about it, if you haven't seen it? Doctor, what do you know about it, if you haven't seen these?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President at least as translated, that question doesn't seem to make such sense. The witness has explained that he was told that the -- there was an enormous quantity of material and that raised a practical issue, in terms of him being able to meaningfully use it. The question as interpreted, "Doctor what do you know about it, if you haven't seen it?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the question was whether the witness knew about the deeper sources having to do with the facts, rather than with the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. psychiatric implications. I think the question is related to that. The witness also said that the deeper sources are to do with the facts rather than the psychiatric implications. So I do understand the question as such, as Mr. Piletta-Zanin wants to know how the witness could be aware of that without ever having seen the, well, the statements as a whole or the material as a whole. I think that is what the question was about. I don't know whether you understood it that way and you maintain your objection, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, it just doesn't seem to be going to any sensible issue. It seems fundamentally the issue is whether Mr. Turner should have been given the entire transcript or not. And if not --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that is not the issue. That is not the purpose of this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Understand and express what Mr. Piletta-Zanin has in mind. The witness has told us that he was not much troubled by not having seen all the material because he was aware of, apart from the practical effects, also he was aware that, well, let's say, the bulk would have to be with the facts rather than the psychiatric aspects of it. And the question of Mr. Piletta-Zanin is, how the witness knows that the bulk of the material would deal with the facts. So to put it rather bluntly,, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you would like to know how Dr. Turner knows that not most of the material was not about the facts, but about the psychiatric impacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you please answer my question, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: My assumption is that most of the material would be about facts and I draw attention to the difference which is pointed out in paragraph 9 of my report about facts and the implications of those fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Doctor, I don't have an impression that you answered my question. You -- what I asked was: How did you know it? Am I to understand from your answer that this was purely hypothetical on your part, that aside from some excerpts that you received. The rest made no difference for your expert report. Is that what it is?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I have said. In answer to your question, that I made an assumption, and I tried to make that assumption clear in the body of my report and in evidence today. I think what I tried to do in my report is to draw a distinction between the facts which are to do with the Court in its determination and if those facts were broadly set out, what would the implications have been, based on international literature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, I believe that my question still has not been answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Interrupt you. Is it your point that, by accepting selected materials, materials selected by the Prosecutor's office, Dr. Turner might have missed relevant information or is it the point that the vast majority of the material in the hands of the Prosecutor is directly relevant for the psychiatric aspects of the case? I mean, we are talking about facts. That means, who was the mayor, when was he mayor, where do you live, when were you born. Is it -- make your point and it is quite clear that if you have not seen all the material, you cannot, on the basis of knowledge of all the material, say anything about what is relevant and not. The witness has testified already that it was an assumption. And I think the -- but, if I am not correct please correct me -- it seems that it is your point already for some 10 or 15 minutes that the selection of the material might have influenced the report of the expert witness. If that is your point, it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my point is the following: Unfortunately, I am not a psychiatric expert, but let me please finish. But I am certain that there are elements that are escaping us on the side of the Defence, us poor lawyers, but perhaps a psychiatric expert by seeing them could perhaps deduce more important things. However, since he did not have these elements, therefore, the entire structure falls down. That is the point that we are developing here. But I am going to go on to another line of questioning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Doctor, you gave a definition of terror here. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I have already said I gave a definition of terror.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. You used a terror campaign, that is what -- these are the terms that you used. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You used it in item 7 of your report. Please go to it. I will read it if I need to.

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I am referring there not to a definition of terror, but I am referring to the indictment which refers to a campaign of shelling and sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Doctor, am I to conclude, therefore, that you espouse this thesis of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Doctor, you used the term "campaign." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... The witness testified that what he does under paragraph 7, that's how it starts: "The indictment refers to," and then I understand that not only the first sentence, but also the second sentence of paragraph 7 is reflecting what is in the indictment. That is what the testimony is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether it is true or not, is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Doctor, did you thought it was useful -- did you think it was useful to give a definition or a clarification on what a campaign is?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: No. I didn't give a definition of a campaign. That is not something which I thought was to the heart of what I had been instructed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Doctor, would you agree with me to consider that the events in Sarajevo are relevant both for a civilian civil war and also for an urban war?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I am not quite sure what that means. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Which one of the two propositions disturbs you? Is it perhaps both?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I don't understand the sentence as is translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Doctor, would you agree with me, just before the break, to say that the events in Sarajevo were relevant, were constituent parts of a civil war and at the same time, of an urban war?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: You are asking me to say whether I agree with facts of a case, using what I presume to be legally defined terms. I think I would like clarification on that before I could answer. I am not sure that this is material, as an expert psychiatrist, that goes to my evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, and beyond that, I think it has been made abundantly clear that the witness has had made available to him aspects of the evidence, not the entire evidence, and, therefore, the question as presently phrased would seem to be based on an inappropriate presumption. There is no suggestion that he has had access to sufficient material to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and apart from that, the witness, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is saying that it is not within his expertise to agree upon the events to have been part of both a civil war and an urban war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Mr. President, but however he could, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has said that it is not within his expertise. So I don't think we should force him to given an answer of something he says he doesn't know about. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But it seems it is time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Adjourn until 20 minutes pas 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I see that you are on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wished to indicate that given the estimate by the Defence, it seems that we will finish today well short of 7.00. With your leave, Mr. President, I don't seek to call the next witness today. There are some particular measures which would make it appropriate, I think, for him to be called tomorrow, if that is acceptable to you, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that that would be a practical solution, yes. So let's first see at what time we do stop and how much time we still have left. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, my question which I would like to ask again is the following: Were you -- did you try to find out if the conditions of a so-called terror are different in an urban environment, and in at times of civil war, than in an extra-urban area and under different circumstances of a civil war?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: What I have tried to set out are factors likely to increase the feeling of terror. Some of those may go to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: We will come to that in a minute. Thank you. Doctor you have told us in your document that you referred to various historical situations. You refer to the Holocaust and to the situation in Cambodia, in 3132. Would you consider that those two aspects, those two historical facts, were also part of a terror campaign?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I can give a personal answer to that, but it seems to me that that is what, if I understand my instruction correctly, that is the definition that Court has to achieve. And I am not sure whether I should go further on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me first see in what way exactly you used the -- that was -- could you give us the number --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3132.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are writing about --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And 35, as far as the Holocaust is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you referred to publications about Cambodia and about the Holocaust. Of course, I do not know exactly what is in these publications, apart from the way you dealt with it. If you feel that, on the basis of your personal knowledge of these situations, or on the basis of your expertise, whether or not based on these publications you could answer the question, I invite you to do so. If you say it is just a personal impression of what I got from the newspapers, then, please tell us, because then under these circumstances, your expertise does not make it possible for you to answer that question, and we would rather not have any guesses as answers to questions, but rather either personal knowledge or the result of you expertise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. From what I know of the literature in Cambodia, for example, there was wide-scale, systematic persecution of people for example, people wearing spectacles because they were deemed to have a level of education. The persecution and the mass killing that I know from the literature took place there, I would regard as consistent with terrorisation of the community. Similarly for those involved in the Holocaust, where there was again mass killing and persecution of people, I personally would see that as another act consistent with terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Doctor. Doctor, in the same vein, is -- was the bombing and the killing of civilians in Nagasaki is also considered a campaign of terror.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to the question on the basis of relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is, I think that history should examine those files in the same case as others. And if every time the Defence wishes to ask a question about a victor's camp, well, I think that the dice have been cast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not on the basis of a lack of relevance at this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. very moment, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that the Chamber would sustain the objection. On the other hand, you are asking about a campaign of terror. I again would like to stress that if the witness knows anything about it, and perhaps we should not go through the whole history and all bad situations, but if you know anything specific or if your expertise could tell us something about Hiroshima, but Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I already tell you that we are not going through a 1000 years back, but Hiroshima f you could tell us something about it. And then not specifically whether it was a campaign of terror. You may say whether you consider it to be terror or not, but the specific words of this indictment are mainly for the Chamber to decide whether it was a campaign of terror or not. But if your expertise could tell us something about it, please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think what I -- with your permission, would like to do, is to try to draw out some of the differences that may exist, where I think I can comment. I don't think I can give personal, professional, scientific answer to that question. I think that some of the differences that may exist between on the one hand the Holocaust and the persecution of the Jews and others, on the one hand, or Cambodia on the one hand, and Hiroshima and Nagasaki on the other hand. Well, I think that there is a difference of persistence. The one -- on the one hand we have events that took place over a prolonged period of time. We have events in which there was the common perception that there was a malicious deliberate persecution of people as people, rather than as occupants of a town at war. So I think that, if I can answer that as best I can, I would say that there were differences between those two sorts of experience which I can comment on. On the other hand I would say it seems likely to me, I can't quote literature because the literature following Hiroshima and Nagasaki has tended to focus much more on physical reactions, but it seems likely to me that those experiences would have been intensely frightening. As I say, the difference would have been perhaps the perception and the persistence, and those are psychological concepts which I try to draw out in the body of my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarification. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, now it is clear. Page 39, line 2, it was stated in the text and not in the transcript. So what I said was a victor's camp and not a camp. Now I shall continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand that. Is that something that I need to know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. It is just that part of the French text spoken by Mr. Piletta-Zanin was not properly brought into the transcript in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Doctor, when you refer to historic situations, could you tell me, because you referred to the Holocaust period, whether you know what the Stukas [phoen] were?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I don't know what the Stukas [phoen] were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: May I help you. Do you know whether the Stukas [phoen] were a weapon, that is a fighter plane, as far as I know, it is a plane that bombs and the military authorities had added to the cockpit of the pilot a siren to create a noise aimed at alarming the population. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Is it true, as far as you know -- I withdraw that. I would like to rephrase the question. Were you told, yes or no, that the Serb forces would -- was theoretically possible would have modified the mortars in order not to make mortars noisy, so as to alarm the population?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I don't recall being told as a fact that mortars were modified, if I understand this, to make this less noisy. No, I don't recall being told that. I don't believe I was told that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Not less noisy, more noisy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you please look at the English translation in the transcript, because I think it does not appear as you intended it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite possible, but it is difficult to see in English it says -- "make mortar noisy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were told in order "not to make mortars noisy" when I did understand it well the question was whether the witness was told that the mortars were made noisy in order to alert the people of their possible arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, to terrorise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You were not informed of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were not informed of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I am sorry. Just wait for a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: It is not in your notes.

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: In that case, I wasn't told that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, now I would like to come back to a more sensitive issue, that of imagination. Could one say that, as a rule, man can fear more that which he does not know, that is, what he imagines, for the simple reason because he will attribute to the fears a greater proportion than would have been the case if he were able to see the object of his fear? I expect that you have understood my question.

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: There are different elements to the question. I think the evidence is that man will fear an event which is unpredictable. In that sense an event which he does not know, I don't think that the evidence is that a man will fear an event which is in imagination, more than an event in reality. In fact, I think the evidence would be to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, Doctor. Now, I would like to quote the following example. If I take the noise of a shelling exploding, is it not true, and I think that is what you told us, that I -- is it not correct that my fear, my anxiety and then my fear, would be much greater as long as I had not seen the damage caused by such an explosion and I wouldn't have been able to see whether my people close to me were in a secure situation or were affected by the explosion?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: Again, it is a complex question. It seems to have a number of elements it. If there was a shelling which I think may have affected my family, and that is described in my report, in one of the snapshot pieces, the lack of knowledge about whether my family had been affected is likely to be a very frightening, very worrying experience. If, on the other hand, the question is that would the reality of a shelling be more or less frightening, then the imagination of a shelling, than the reality would be more frightening, in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. But is it not true that man is relieved, consequently, if he can see the reality of the explosion of a shell and that his family had not been affected?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: It is like saying, if I go to a sale and make a bargain. The shelling isn't likely to be associated with relief. It is a question of how bad it is. If, at the time of a shelling, someone has an overriding worry about the welfare of their family, then it might be less bad once they realise their family is safe. But I don't think we can say that that is a factor of relief, in any way that I would understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Doctor --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the General and I cannot hear the translation on channel 6. Not following the channel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it solved?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is already for the French booth, for the English booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it has been solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is all right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you please repeat what you have just said so as to have the translation in Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: How far back?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps from "if at the time of a shelling.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If, at the time of a shelling, someone has an overriding worry about the welfare of their family, then it might be less bad once they realise their family is safe. But I don't think that we can say that that is a factor of relief in any way that I would understand that. It is a question of being less bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Witness, when you carried out your expertise, did you look at a map?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: Probably. I do have a map of the Balkans on my office wall at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Map of the Balkans that is rather broad. A map of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: No, I did not look at a map of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know what the hearing range of a shell of 60, 82 and 102 -- 120 millimetres?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am a psychiatrist, so the answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the answer is no. Yes, that is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. I know the witness is an expert in psychiatric and I am asking him this question for a specific reason. Do you know, in terms of distance, what the breadth of the city of Sarajevo is?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, can you rule out, in front of this court, that when the firing, when the shots of mortars reached the lines of separation or confrontation, these shots could not have been heard inside the city and, therefore create a stress?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I can make no comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But I would like you to do so. If you don't know about it, then can you please tell us that you don't know?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I don't know. I am a psychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that you are a psychiatrist, Doctor, but you did not examine in your report, expert report, the range, the so-called in some way collateral range of the effect of firing of mortar firing on the, strictly speaking, peripheral military targets?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I don't understand what peripheral military targets are. I just want to repeat the answer I have already given, which is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think what Mr. Piletta-Zanin would like to know from you is that the sound of shelling with a purely military character, that means directed against people at the front line, whether you took into consideration that the sound of the shelling might have contributed to the feelings of the civilian population, therefore, not directly attacked by the shelling but nevertheless being confronted with it. That is, I think, what Mr. Piletta-Zanin --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, on the level of the noise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... The sound.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
