utterances.text: What I have said is that in time of war, civilians caught up in warfare, in paragraph 31, perhaps because they live close to a military target, will be affected by this experience. However, where there is systematic targeting or whether it is over and above that, for example, where they may be seen as a malicious and horrifying act, it is more likely to cause a more marked fear reaction. Now, I can't say where the threshold is. I believe that is a matter for the Court. What I can say is that the closer you get to one end of the scale, the more likely it is that there will be extreme fear or terror.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. But, Witness, very briefly, it is true that in your report, expert report, you did not take into consideration this particular aspect, that is, on the issue of the perimetric, quote unquote, that is, of the trenches and of the lines of separation?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. At a given point you spoke of hospitals. Do you know in your capacity as a psychiatrist, do you know for a city of 350.000 inhabitants, do you know what were the daily entries in hospitals in times of peace, in terms of when accidents happened, what were the entries in hospitals, admissions to hospitals?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: Again, there are two elements to that, I think. One is a normative question; what would be the normal expected rate. That simply doesn't exist. I mean, there are wide variations in normative rates from country to country and I am being asked as a psychiatrist, I think here, not about psychiatric admissions but about surgical admissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I have to interrupt you. If you don't know it, then please say that you don't know it, for reasons of time.

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: The second point of the question is what were the rates in Sarajevo and I don't know that. The second part is there isn't a normative figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I maintain to say that I never spoke of Sarajevo in my question.

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: That is why I was trying to answer what seemed to be a question -- I am sorry I would --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, but I would like you to wait for my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has testified from country to country that there were wide varieties and if he says something about what he doesn't know or what he doesn't know, then he says: "As far as Sarajevo is concerned, I don't know." That means Sarajevo would be different perhaps than what happens in England or in the United States. So I don't think that it is a mere fact that you didn't mention Sarajevo in your question makes it illogical to refer to Sarajevo. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do you know how many hospitals there were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I don't. I have read literature, for example, the paper by Pretto which describes surgical hospitals, but I can't tell you a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, does the figure of admissions in terms of accidents, admissions for accidents in the time of war in hospitals in Sarajevo, does the figure of under one for a thousand, out of a thousand, less than one, would this figure seem to you very high considering that we are talking about civilians and military personnel together?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I -- what I do know is that at time of war, there is an increased rate of accident. I know that because that applies to British troops stationed in war or peace-keeping zones. And I know that because I know the psychological injuries which follow. I can't comment on the surgical accident rate in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So whether the numbers mentioned by Mr. Piletta-Zanin are relatively high or low --

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I can't comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can't comment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would require a surgeon, I believe, to give Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. expert testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say it is beyond you expertise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, you said, within the framework of your expertise, that the question of shortage of gas, water, electricity that this was something that could be part of this campaign, this is the term that you used, that is part of this campaign of terror. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: Would you draw me to the paragraph where I say that, because I don't think I did say it in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: That could be a problem of interpretation, but I think you said it, on one hand, in item 6, line 2 and also in your conclusions at the end, in your findings in the end of your paper, of your document. You said it somewhere that it was in the middle of the conclusion under 41. I think here "it is quite obvious that if there was a disruptions in supply of food and water..." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. What -- maybe it is the interpretation, but the question that I have is within the framework of my expertise, the question of shortage of gas, water and electricity were something that could be part of this campaign, this campaign of terror. What is set out in paragraph 41 is really a summary of what I would do or, if I thought someone had a primary purpose of inducing terror, what they might do, on the basis of psychological evidence. I am not inferring a fact. What I would do, or I think they would do, is they would try to do a number of things, including disrupting supplies of food and water and disrupting medical services. But that is a psychological answer rather than a factual answer, if the Court understands the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, sir, if what you are saying, is it also valid for gas and electricity? You are talking about supply of water. Is it the same reasoning would then apply for gas and electricity, is that true?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: What I have done in this report is essentially to try and draw out those factors which are likely to increase the severity of emotional impacts, factors likely to increase difficulty include concurrent stressors, heat, noise, illness, fatigue, and so on. Disruption of gas and electricity supplies are likely to have that sort of effect. It doesn't mean that those factors are essential factors, but if it those factors were involved then it would be likely to increase an effect on a civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Doctor, are you therefore saying that if someone, since you have put it hypothetically, if someone had taken a decision to cut these supplies or not authorise their supply, these people whoever they are, would have then participated in a plan of terror, partially or fully?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: Not necessarily. It may be that supplies are disrupted in warfare for all sorts of reasons. But what I would say, if there was a primary purpose of causing terror, then that would be something which would be an act that someone might wish to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say that it is quite useful asset to create terror, if you want to create terror.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But I wouldn't -- but of course these supplies in warfare may be cut off for other reasons and one can't infer a motivation. But it would be a useful asset to follow, I agree entirely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, we are going on to another point. You mentioned on several occasions and the item 15 of your document, you were talking about a shelling of -- random shelling. Where does this terminology come from, that is my first question, random shelling?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: It probably comes from me. I wrote this report. I think what I am trying to draw out here is that actions likely to cause high arousal, fatigue, sleeplessness, and therefore, my comment would be that random shelling, it could have been excessive shelling or persistent shelling, but random shelling also would be likely to cause people to be fatigued and sleepless. That was trying to link to those two statements together.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Doctor. Since you spoke of and you gave some examples of shellings or firing, I would like us to give you here now, before this Chamber, one example of a random shelling or two examples or three examples, could you do that? Could you do that?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I think -- I suppose a simple answer is, if you want me to quote facts to the Tribunal, the answer is probably no. But that wasn't what I was trying to do when I wrote this section of my report. What I was trying to do was to say to the Tribunal, if these facts as alleged are found to be broadly true, and if there was disruption of people's ability to sleep, state of illness, state of arousal, then that would be a factor likely to cause an increase in fear and persistence of fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir how could you know first of all, that there were -- there was random shelling in Sarajevo, first question? Did you base yourself solely on what the Prosecution told you?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: No. There are descriptions of shelling in Sarajevo. Those descriptions appear to be random. But I don't think that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, I am going to interrupt you. I am sorry. I apologise. I am going to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Let the witness finish his answer. Please proceed Mr. -- Yes. I am addressing you in the wrong way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I should say please proceed, Dr. Turner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is fine. What I was going to say is: I don't think that it is for me to say if there was random shelling in Sarajevo. What I am saying here is that if there was random shelling in Sarajevo, then this is the psychological impact that I would expect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, you said and that is the reason why I wanted to interrupt you, you said there were descriptions of shellings in Sarajevo. What are these descriptions? Where did they come from? What are your sources? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I can't point you to -- I mean I have read descriptions of shelling in a number of sources. For example, some of the material that I have --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, I am going to have to stop you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the witness is explaining to us what his sources were. That is your question. "What are your sources, could you tell us." So he is now explaining it to us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you want me to try to give a quotation pointing to those shellings being random, I can't. I can't recall such a quotation. But I have read descriptions of shelling in Sarajevo. What I was trying to do here is to say that if there were shelling which was either random and therefore disruptive or which was in some way determined to disrupt sleep or cause high arousal or illness, psychologically. So psychological elements was what I was trying to focus on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. What are your sources, could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I think I have already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness has testified -- has answered the question to the extent that he say he can't give a precise source of where random shelling is part of it. But perhaps we could make a distinction, would the sources comprise both the evidentiary material provided to you by the Office of the Prosecutor and descriptions you found in literature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least we have -- so two areas of source. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But, however, Witness, you cannot now quote one article, one piece of work, one reference that would have described such alleged random shelling?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I have already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, I am going to interpret that as having already answered that question. Thank you. Sir, do you know if, yes or no, in the city of Sarajevo there was a high number of military target?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I don't know the number of military targets in Sarajevo. I find it hard to comment on whether they were high or low. I presume there were some.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then would you please proceed to your next issue, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Were you informed of the existence of mobile military targets in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I believe that I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What were you told?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: Simply that there were such targets. It was relevant in the question of proportionality. But that is a legal question, not a psychiatric one. But it was important that I understood that civilians could be affected by shelling of military targets. I can't say that I recall any more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for your answer. Now I would like to go to the question of snipers. I believe that I detected a contradiction in your report. You said that what would have created terror is the fact that there was this unpredictability aspect; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: Unpredictability is a factor that Rachman cites and others cite as a factor likely to cause increased distress, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask, "imprevisible" and "unpredictable," Unpredictable, whether that is exactly the same to me or not. The translation was "unpredictable" and the question was "imprevisible". Could you please be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the answer can be given by me, then I believe that I can say that it is equivalent translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: However, sir, you, at some point, you tell us that point 17 of your document, you quoted some of the statements that were given to you and in which it is established that as a rule people knew where the marksmen were firing from. This is page 6, first paragraph, of the statement by Dr. Mandilovic. And the first sentence says the following, I will quote in English. [In English] "You could know approximately where sniper fire was coming from. And you would be able to project yourself, to see that you were not out in an open space, facing the southern side." [Interpretation] Isn't it true that this unpredictable character, this feature, was specifically demonstrated by this quote which says that, one, they knew where the firing was coming from; and two, that they knew, they knew how to protect themselves and I am talking about the snipers?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I think the point of the quotation as far as I understand it and the point that I thought I was trying to illustrate was to do with shelling, that this particular witness was talking about their experience of sniping and shelling and saying as far as I can see that the fact that shelling by contrary, or by contrast that shelling is unpredictable made it worse. So what he goes on to say is the projectiles of shells, you can't save yourself from projectiles of shells because they come in in an arch and they are dispersed and their destructive power is greater than a gunshot. However, that was to apply that that was a worse experience and I think that is illustrated the fact that Rachman was pointing to intensity and unpredictability. This particular witness, I think, was also commenting on their own experience of unpredictability and intensity. But it's an illustration. Again, that's all I can make of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, I believe that you did not answer my question. Is it true, according to this quote, that you yourself chose, this feature of unpredictability and this ineluctable feature of sniper fire was not illustrated by this quote, which actually says the opposite. "We know how to protect ourselves, we know where it is coming from, we know how to protect ourselves." Isn't that what it says here?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I think I did answer the question. This particular quotation does illustrate a predictable feature of sniper fire, according to this witness. What the witness seems to be saying, as far as I understand it, this quotation, is that the greater distress was caused by the unpredictable experience. That was the psychological element that I was trying to go to. And I think that's my answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In fact, the question is, Dr. Turner, but it is perhaps not so easy to understand, the question is: Since Dr. Mandilovic has described sniper situations as a relatively predictable and he is describing a situation where you can at least protect yourself against it, that sniping, as it happened on the basis of this description would not have contributed to the terror. I think that is the basis of the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that what I would say to that is -- I am sorry I am answering the long answer again. But what I would say to that is no single factor is likely to be -- to give an explanation for a state of terror. Likely there are a number of factors. In this context, I am looking at intensity and unpredictability as two factors. My presumption is that if someone were to snipe at me and miss me very narrowly I would find that a very frightening experience on the basis of intensity. If it happened repeatedly, I would probably still find that a very frightening experience on the basis of intensity. What wouldn't be there, necessarily, on this statement would be unpredictability. But I wouldn't say unpredictability was an essential criteria or indeed that any of these was an essential criteria. The cumulative effect of a number of criteria is likely to be relevant in gauging the degree terror produced by a set of actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned in your report that an attack programme that was repeated on a civilian population, carried out on a considerable scale could produce this terror, could result in terror. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: Could you point me to the paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I don't have it on top of my head, but I believe you would know?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I think the trouble is, it is a very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please find the place, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to go to another question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You mentioned, in paragraph 20, the fact that cultural images or icons were also targeted and that this was characteristic of this mechanism that we are talking about, this is mentioned in point 20. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you ever told, Doctor, that in this hospital, on the top floors of this hospital, there was a small group of people with weapons led by a captain and that from that location they were carrying out attacks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It is an interesting proposition which unfortunately was not put to any of the three witnesses who gave evidence that they either worked or lived in the State Hospital. One of them indeed said that he lived in the top floors. For that reason, that it hasn't been put, my respectful submission, it certainly couldn't be put to this witness or implied to this witness that that is a piece of information he should have been aware of. And in any event, because it hasn't been put and should have been to the earlier witnesses, the Defence should be stopped from putting their proposition. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you indicate where we find a source for this proposition?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give it to you now in order not to waste time, but I will do it later. But I will continue with the same line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, you said that the Kosevo hospital was deliberately targeted. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. What I quote is the report in the medical literature, describing the Kosevo hospital. I don't say that it was deliberately targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Wait a minute. You did not put in your report that you considered that the Kosevo hospital was deliberately targeted?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would be grateful if my learned colleague could, when he refers to the report, state the relevant paragraph so that we can all see exactly what the words are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please indicate what paragraph you are referring to, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to find it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Turner, if you would remember where we find in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the report what you just said there was, then you can perhaps assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just found reference to the report by Jones, which was paragraph 36, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that be the same source, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Mr. President. I was going to say this now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, you wrote the following [In English]: "In Kosevo hospital in Sarajevo, there was evidence of deliberate targeting."

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: Can you point me to the line, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I will indeed give you the line. This is four, five, six, seven, lines four, five, six, seven.

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Didn't you write that, and you signed this, that the Kosevo hospital was deliberately targeted by fire?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: No. What I am quoting is a report by Dr. Jones and I put this particular phrase in quotations to make it absolutely plain it is a quotation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- That was clear to everyone that the expert witness in this report is describing here, not his own personal knowledge, but that he is referring to the report of Dr. Jones. So what is the use of, I would say, misquoting?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I wasn't going to misquote, but the witness incorporated this statement into his expert report. Therefore, he made it his own, he is taking conclusions from it, so he has made it his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Were you never told sir, that as far as the Kosevo hospital is concerned, there were acts of military provocation by other parties?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: No, I don't recall being told that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Nobody ever told you that there was firing, there was shots that came originated from the Kosevo hospital in the direction of other parties?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: No, I don't recall being told that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The evidence has been consistent throughout that shots fired -- the shots were fired from the grounds of Kosevo Hospital, not from the buildings themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that is the way I understood the question as a matter of fact. But I think the witness has twice said that he was not informed about it. So, please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: We are now coming to your conclusions soon, sir. Sir, you spoke of random shelling by using, I believe the idea of frequency, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: No. I commented in the paragraph that we were looking at before. Let me see if I can find it again. It would be helpful to go back to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Paragraph 15, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Paragraph 15. What I was commenting on there, as a matter of clarification to the Court, was that what I was interested in were actions likely to cause high arousal, illness, fatigue or sleeplessness, because I was citing those as factors illustrated by Rachman in his important paper. Now random shelling would be a factor which seems likely to me, if it existed, and I am not saying it did exist, but if it existed, would be a factor likely to lead to sleeplessness and fatigue. In illustrating that to the Court, I also said that frequent shelling might have a similar effect. So either of those would be of relevance. What I am interested in primarily is the psychological construct which I am trying to illustrate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. You used on page 58, line 3, to be accurate, the notion of "intensity."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You cannot look back on the transcript. We can see, we have laptops. It was -- I will read to you literally what is in the transcript. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I have got on line -- on page 58, line 3 and I will read the whole: "In this context, I am looking at intensity and unpredictability as two factors. My presumption is that if someone were to snipe at me and miss me very narrowly, I would find that a very frightening experience, on the basis of intensity." So the word, "intensity" has been used in this context. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you used the term, "intensity" regarding the sniping, but I think that in regard to shelling, indiscriminate shelling, the criteria would be the same; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: Both shelling and sniping can be associated with an intense trauma experience, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for your answer. Consequently, Witness, were you told, yes or no, from 1993, end of 1993, that the Serb side, not only sought to obtain a peace agreement, but also to obtain the demilitarisation of Sarajevo; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: No, that hasn't been part of my instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, is it true that a will, not only expressed in ceasefire, in terms of ceasefire, but also in terms of demilitarisation and peace, is necessarily contradictory - in contradiction - with the idea of shelling?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] Indiscriminate shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- I object to the question for a number of reasons. Firstly, it is outside the expertise of the witness, I would suggest; secondly, it presumes that the interest on the Serb side in negotiating peace from 1993 is inconsistent with maintaining a shelling and sniping campaign against Sarajevo and civilians, if the other side did not agree to the peace. And that is a matter, firstly, of evidence and certainly not a proposition which the Prosecution accepts the evidence establishes. That being the case, the question lacks any probative value, as well as being outside the expertise of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the objection is sustained, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. If you want to touch upon the issue, you should do it in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I will rephrase the question. Were you informed, Witness, of the number of daily shelling taking place in Sarajevo in 1992?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I haven't been given the numbers of daily shelling in Sarajevo in any of the relevant years.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, consequently you were not able to examine because you were not provided this, possible drastic decrease in the number of shelling between 1992 and 1994, for instance?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. That is a matter of fact, which I haven't focused on in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, the same question in relation to the decrease in the number of wounded or deceased for 1993, compared to 1993 and then compared to 1994?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I have access to some figures about the number of wounded and deceased in the report for example by Pretto in the open literature. That deals with a period covering part of 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But this stopped here and you were not given other elements. So 1993, 1994.

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I wasn't given any of those elements. I did a search of the medical literature, in order to obtain my own information. That is where the paper by Pretto came from. It wasn't given to me by anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, consequently, not having been given those elements, you were not able to do anything else but to make hypotheses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I don't think my paper is hypothetical. It draws out the scientific literature in psychology and psychiatry and those conclusions I don't think are hypothetical conclusions. Their relevance to Sarajevo is pre-- is predicated upon the facts of the case. To that degree, the paper has to be cautioned and qualified and I have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I didn't refer to the scientific elaboration of your report. I was referring to in terms of its application to the realities of Sarajevo and here we should agree, I think, that in relation to Sarajevo, this is comparatively hypothetical?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: My understanding is that, for the purpose of this issue, the only people who can determine what those realities were is the Tribunal. That is how we started out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I think altogether we have spent some 20 minutes at least in cross-examination in order to establish that the expert witness has based his expert report on the assumption that the information that is given to him would be correct information. And to start another play of words on whether this is hypothetical or based on an assumption is not of great use at this moment. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will come back to your conclusions, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: That is, paragraph 41 of your document, where you say, for instance, and I believe it is in a hypothetical form, the fact of opening fire on cemeteries would be one way of obtaining that objective and accomplishing it. I think this is somewhere at the end of paragraph 41.

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: What I say in paragraph 41, relevant to cemeteries, is that -- well, I think I have to start by quoting the beginning. "If someone had a primary purpose of inducing terror in a civilian population, the literature reviewed here would suggest the following." And then in paragraph 41 I go through a number of elements. Towards the end I say: "The assault -- I talk about attempts to increase emotional tension. And then I go on to say as one of these factors the assault would be designed to create emotional overload perhaps by interfering with normal grieving processes. Sniping at cemeteries would be possible to achieve this. Any means to produce a feeling of helplessness or a sense of vulnerability would be followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. The information that you had in relation to the firing on cemeteries, where did they come from? Are they the same, from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I believe that I had that information. I was certainly aware of allegations that there had been firing on cemeteries from news reports. So that goes well before the Prosecution. I am not citing that and I am not saying that there was firing on cemeteries. I believe that there was information in the witness -- from the witness statements showing that there was firing on cemeteries. But again, we need to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we now see how the witness struggles with your question because you don't put to him what seems to be, or what at least I have to take it that would be the Defence case. Of course, he is guessing on what you want to know. Perhaps many other people in this case would know. Why don't you put to the witness what you want to ask him?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is very simple. Where did he get that information from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Several, several, several times how he got this information. He has now explained to us that the firing on the cemeteries might have been known to him from news reports before. And he says. Now please come to your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I was making a distinction. The first intervention was, I think, related to shelling and this one is clearly related to sniping. And these are two totally distinct points. And my second point was to establish whether the sources were the same in respect of sniping, and I think it is quite normal that the Prosecution should do -- that the Defence -- sorry -- should do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please come to your point, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Is it true, Witness, that as regards both shelling and sniping incidents, that you -- basically you received information from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I have received -- it is the same answer -- I have received information from the Prosecution. I have consulted the medical press. Clearly I have knowledge through news reports. It is the same answer that I have given consistently. What I try to focus on here is the psychological implication of events that may or may not happened and are for the Tribunal to determine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Were you, yes or no, told by the Prosecution that it would seem that the utilities in terms of water, gas and electricity, were sometimes disrupted by the Muslim officials in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: No, I don't recall being told that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, were you told whether near to the population and the places in fighting of the town or in the surroundings of the town, there were important military -- significant numbers of military force in terms of manpower?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I believe I have already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Any men were on the Muslim side as far as you were considered, under arms?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... The expertise of the witness, totally beyond his report. Please proceed to your next point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to confer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the General believes that we are not beyond the scope of expertise because if it would so happen that, at Sarajevo, a considerable number of soldiers were located in the city and were able to have been considered, in certain moments and in certain places, legitimate military targets, then that element should have been placed -- put at the disposal of the expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... The question is whether it is all about. The question is whether your report and your conclusions, based upon the facts as you received them, would be different if, in the city of Sarajevo, the population was rather mixed, that means to a large extent, military and civilian all mixed together. Would that change your report and conclusions, and in what way would it change your conclusions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think -- I don't know that it would change my report very much, but it would change the implications of my report for the Court. If the -- if the same actions took place and the civilians were effected in exactly the same way, whether on the one hand there were soldiers and on the other hand, there were no soldiers, there probably would be a small difference in that the civilians would appraise or understand the behaviour differently. So there probably would be a difference in terms of their perception of whether or not it was malicious or intended to terrorise. That probably would make a difference. But many of these factors would apply in both situations. So if I can try and draw that to a conclusion, what I think I would say is that if the civilians appraised the situation as being reasonable, there would Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. probably be less effect, but in spite of that, there would be wide-scale civilian fear. If the civilians felt that it was malicious, there probably would be a greater degree of fear. The implication for the Court would be different, of course, because then you come into the question of legal issue of proportionality and so on, which is not for me. But that would be the best answer I think I can give at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, have you ever testified as an expert witness before, in relation to other comparable situations, that is a town in a situation of war?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I don't believe I have given witness evidence about a town in a situation of war, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, is it not true, especially when we speak of a city which is comparatively small in dimensions, and where a war is evolving, that the war is, in itself, a symbol of terror?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: What I have said in this report and I think it was paragraph 31, is -- and I think I have already quoted this -- "there is a likelihood that civilians caught up in warfare, perhaps because they live close to a military target will be effected by that experience. "However, in my opinion, where civilians are systematically targeted or where the offensive is and over and above that which is explained by normal military objectives, these will be seen as malicious and horrifying acts. These are likely to cause a much more marked fear reaction [terrorisation] in the early phase. And then later in some people, this will be replaced by apathy and despair."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I have only two questions left. One has to do with what you have just quoted, that is, paragraph 31. What do you understand by what you have just said? That is to say at the end of page 15 and beginning of page 16 in using words, "normal military objectives." Could you be more precise, more specific.

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, so you do not know what normal military targets are?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: As I have repeatedly said, I believe that that distinction as to whether there was shelling or sniping at military targets is a matter of fact and a matter for the Court. There are legal issues of proportionality and distinction to be drawn. I don't think that those go to my expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you learned of the indictment and of the pre-trial brief. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As interpreted that question does not make much sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the question is whether you have seen the indictment and the Prosecution's pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first two paragraphs of my record are headed "basis for the report." In paragraph 1, I briefly summarised some of my qualifications. In paragraph 2, I cite some of the source -- I cited the source material that I have been provided with. That is a routine part of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, is your answer yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: In preparing this report, in addition to the reference material, I also had access to extracts from the Prosecutor's trial brief dated October 2001, a copy of the indictment against Stanislav Galic and a number of short extracts of testimony from the trial transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So your answer is yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you had two more questions, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. You are just asking the witness to repeat what he has written unless, and it seems that you easily accept his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was wrong, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Not read it, fine, then I listen to your next questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I asked the witness whether yes or no he had this. The witness wanted to read this out, but an answer, yes or no answer would have been much simpler and that was my last question. And my last question would be as follows:

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, have you, yes or no given your document while you were writing your document, whether you were knew about the pre-trial brief of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think the question is that in your report it says that you had access to the pre-trial brief. I think the question is whether you took access, I mean, whether you have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It may be, Mr. President, that, in fact, the question goes to whether he always had access to the pre-trial brief of the Defence, but in any event, the witness, in reading the sentence from his report, has made it clear that he had access to extracts from the Prosecution's trial brief, not the brief as a whole. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes I see now that you are asking whether he had access to the pre-trial brief of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not if he had access to it, but if he read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you read the pre-trial brief of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Only one question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir you mentioned that the British Medical Journal was a peer review journal. Could you please explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: What it means is that papers presented to the British Medical Journal are sent out to independent reviewers before publication. I can't Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. say whether it applies to any particular paper, but that would be the normal rule of the journal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Are there any qualifications for the independent reviewers?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: They are peer reviewers so they would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I apologise, but there are already problems of translation because of the rapidity of Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since you are speaking the same language, it takes some time to have it all translated. So could you -- the last question was whether there were any qualifications for the independent reviewers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise. But if there are problems of translation, I think I have to mention them for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It so happens that at line 18, the peer paper, that has not been interpreted correctly, the French booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that now the peer paper has been properly translated? Or should I say the peers paper?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see no objections any more, so please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, I was asking you whether you are aware of what qualifications the independent reviewers must have to carry out their task?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: I think what I would like to do for the Court is to answer the question and then add a little clarification, if I may. Peer review means review by scientific equals, so peer reviewers are people who are recognised as experts in a particular field. So the qualification for a review would be expertise. I have about a dozen of papers in my bag to review which I may do some on the plane on the way home. That would be some example of the peer review process. What this usually refers to is material of a scientific nature. That is the clarification that I would wish to add and be sure that I don't mislead the Court. The article by Jones may or may not fall within that strictly scientific definition. That is why I don't know whether it would have been peer reviewed by external reviewers. The British Medical Journal has a staff of doctors, so it would have been reviewed in-house by people familiar with that area. And in fact, the British Medical Journal at that time included people on the staff who were relatively knowledgeable about this sort of area. But what I can't be sure is whether there would have been external peer review of this paper, which I wouldn't wish to mislead.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions. Let me just confer for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I should address the interpreters first. There are two questions from the Bench. We could have a break now and then return at a quarter past 6.00 and then have these two questions. But if you would prefer to translate those two questions and answers, we could continue. May I hear -- I just have to change to one of the interpretation channels. Could the French and/or the English booth and the B/C/S booth inform me what they would prefer. I know it's long.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I think we can continue, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I hear from the English booth that we can continue. I take it that that is the answer of all three booths. Judge Nieto-Navia has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just two questions. The first one is, you mentioned Dr. Aitcheson [Phoen] but as far as I know he is not cited at the end as one of the sources you used. Is it because you read it, but not quoted it or because you read it after writing the report?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: No, I read it and didn't quote. As I recall, that question was about -- I made a comment in paragraph 10 about other reports with similar descriptions and I was asked what other material there was that I hadn't cited. I read it before, but it was in the form of a diary describing his experiences in Bosnia. It didn't include the numbers that the other reports had. It was consistent with them, but I chose to quote the other ones because they gave more detailed information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: My second question is the following: Let's suppose that somebody who was in Sarajevo during this period sees when a shell explodes and kills or injures people, probably some members of his family. According to your report, he or she suffers a trauma. Is it true?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: Depends on what you mean by the word, "trauma" and this may need to be careful in translation. As I would use the word, they suffer -- they experience an event, a traumatic event. It doesn't mean that they develop a trauma response and that is where the wording becomes important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Okay. My question is the following: Is there any difference in that case if the shell is fired by the Serbs surrounding the city, or by the Bosniaks from within the city?

utterances.speaker: STUART TURNER
utterances.text: What I have -- there probably is. But let me try and explain. What I have tried to do in this report is to say that there are a number of factors which may interact and which may operate together. The event of a shell firing, landing, killing other members of the family, well, if I draw your attention to paragraph 29, that is the sort of event which is certainly likely to be traumatic to many people. But what I have tried to do in this report is to say probably there are a number of factors which operate together which lead to a state of terrorisation. And so that particular scenario affecting that particular individual, is likely to run -- is likely to experience extreme fear, distress and to have a persisting reaction to it. That would be consistent with paragraph 29. I am looking at the population, how many people in a population would be affected. It is likely that a count needs to be taken of a whole range of different events. And there I think the perception of that shelling by others, perhaps not so close is important and that for them, their perception, is this is a malicious act, is this part of a campaign, probably does have an influence on the way they react to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Turner, since there are no more questions from the Bench, this concludes your testimony in this court. I thank you very much for having come to The Hague and to have answered questions both of the parties and of the Bench and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please escort Mr. Turner out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did understand that it is of no use to call your next witness any more. That is perhaps one of the reasons why we tried to finish before this break, would mean protective measures to be put in place, et cetera, that is not worthwhile and I take it the witness is not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even if we were to decide otherwise, we would have another problem. That means that we will before adjourning, I take it that the Prosecution tenders or is it -- I am just wondering -- yes, you have given as the number P3716 for the English P3716.1 for the translation in B/C/S. I take it that that this has been tendered in evidence

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Except, Mr. President, it has already been filed so I suppose it is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is without any exhibit number. Let's say P3716 is the number for the filed expert report of Dr. Stuart Turner. Was the translation filed as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that still would have to be admitted into evidence. Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, bearing in mind that the Prosecution is tendering Dr. Turner's report as an exhibit, following the cross-examination of Dr. Turner by the Defence, we object to the tendering of this exhibit, considering that this document is based solely on assumptions of one side, that is, as an expert opinion in finding it is not complete and it is subjective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Having an early break gives the Chamber an advantage of considering it overnight and to give you a decision on this objection by tomorrow. We will then adjourn until tomorrow in the afternoon at a quarter past 2.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
